blocks.x: You ready? I'll see. What is this? This is the fourth reel now. It's a... I think we talked at lunch about meeting Joe Glazer rather than on a tape, if I remember correctly. Maybe so, yeah. And, uh... That's another thing you could mention.
Let's see, we're starting up a few days later. What's today's date on?
Today is November 19th on a Monday morning in the office of Dick Allen at the Tulane archives, Jazz archives. And we're going to get underway and continue this interview.
Yeah, we're continuing with Bob Coquille. Did you notice my tie?
How about that?
Can you see? You got crawfish all over it?
Oh, where did you get that?
Some friends of mine...
That's pretty good, I didn't notice that.

Some friends of mine were in New York at the American Museum of Natural History and they saw this. So they made the sound of the crawfish and bought the tie. See, that's pretty clever. They had been there at that funny thing where I had the jazz band and that... The International Boswell Institute.
Right, where I shot the picture. Where you shot the picture.
Yeah.
Well, I'm sure if my Uncle Walter would have had a chance to get a necktie like that, he'd have probably worn it all the time. Oh, sure.

Well... That's pretty good. You know, something that occurred to me that most people don't ask about, maybe they don't think about things like this, but it strikes me that there's a difference between bands. Some play very clean and some play very rough. Now, playing with the kind of bands you did, what kind of bands do you like?

Well, as I mentioned before, I started out playing dance music and all the dance bands, well they played the regular orchestrations that you would go by at Whirline's or any of the music stores. And occasionally during the night you would fake a few tunes, you know, play some jazz, but 80% of it was reading the regular orchestrations because 90% of the work you would get was for dancing, you see. But we would throw in a few fake tunes without doing any reading at all and just kind of jazz it up a little during the night. But then, in around 1953, I switched over to the Dixieland jazz feel when I started working on Bourbon Street.

Well, some of the players I was listening to yesterday with Connie Jones, I thought they were very smooth. Well, Glenn Wilson, the new clarinet player in town, talking about him. And he'll play very smoothly for a while and then he'll play some really dirty notes, some rough style playing once in a while just to maybe lend a little variety or something. Well, that's possible.
Was he playing saxophone at the time?
No, only clarinet. Or on the clarinet?
Yeah.
And, but on the whole that was a very smooth band. Very clean. And people used to characterize Sharkey's playing as clean. Well, do you like people to play clean or rough or do you like both?

Well, it depends on the group as a whole. Yeah. How they're putting out the music. I think Connie has a, on the whole, as a clean band. I've heard his group and Connie's a wonderful trumpet player. And I'm sure he also has a few charts that have been written out, you know, and well rehearsed and well executed. And of course most of it might be played, you know, without any charts at all, which they're very capable of doing. Yeah. But I know he has some nice arrangements.
Yeah. So, you sometimes wanna hear a band that plays a little rough, gut bucket, and then sometimes smooth. Right.
It depends on the band. The voice of the band, yeah.
No rules.
Yeah. Something to get away from the usual routine of the overnight, you know, jazz.
And then somebody sits in. Keeps it from getting monotonous.
Give them a little variety. Sometimes I like bands that play out of tune and bad notes and everything, you know.
Not too bad. I can still enjoy them. Not too bad. Not too bad.
Not too bad.
Not too bad. Not too bad.
Not too often.
Well, a lot of good musicians are willing to take chances.
Well, that's true.
And they'll fluff a few notes to try a new idea.

That's true, very true, because jazz gives you the opportunity to express yourself freely, you know, and try and stay within a chord structure of that particular tune at the same time. But it gives you a chance to express your own feelings towards that particular tune that you're playing without worrying about reading music, but still staying within a chord structure of that particular number.

You brought us some pictures, too. Another thing that I wanted to talk about. And why don't we look at the ones of people like Al Streaming? All right. And you can tell me about them. You have stuff written on the back, but you may think of more.

Well, let's see. Some of these, I can't remember exactly when they were taken. Now, this one was taken probably, I would assume, probably during the 30s. And it's a photograph that I shot myself up on a Jung roof, which I think nowadays is what, the Grand Hotel? It was a brand of change later to the Brand Hotel. Now I think it's the Grand Hotel.
Well, anyway, in the old days, it was a Jung Hotel.

And the Jung Hotel had a beautiful roof garden up there where they held a lot of dances up on a Jung roof. They also had a beautiful room down on the bottom called the Florentine Room on the main floor. But a lot of the dances were held up on a Jung roof in the old days back in the 30s and late 20s and early 30s and late 30s for that matter. And this shot, a photograph I shot up on a Jung roof. And it shows Al Streaming standing up and Leon Fellman on drums and Leon Krasnoff on saxophone. I can't remember two of the sax players. And it shows Eddie Dusan, who is today a practicing attorney, a very fine attorney. He's holding up my bass fiddle because I took the photograph. And next to Eddie is his brother Irving, Irvin Dusan, who's currently president of Columbia Homestead, who gave up music many years back. But he was a very fine trumpet man. Both the Dusan boys were very fine trumpet players.
May I look at it? Mm-hmm. Say that you're not in the picture because you took it.

No. This one holding up the bass, the string bass, is Eddie Dusan. He's a practicing attorney today. And the fellow right next to him is Irvin Dusan, who today is president of Columbia Homestead and hasn't played music in a number of years.
Al Estraticos used to play on the Jung roof, I think.
Right.
They had that big convention facility in there, that huge ballroom.

Right. And they had that big two-lane room. That's probably the room you're speaking of. Maybe so that I... Two-lane room is a tremendous room. Well, I think it holds about 1,500 people because there are many bigger rooms now today and other buildings that have since been constructed.
That's only recently that there have been bigger rooms, is there I remember?

Oh, yeah, in the last few years. Well, today you have, what, out on the riverfront, Rivergate, which is a tremendous place, and you have the Superdome, which, oh my goodness, you have all kinds of places nowadays.
But for a hotel, the Jung surely, for a big convention, it was the one that they had to use. Oh, yeah.
That's what I'm getting at.
That's what I'm getting at. They had that work.
The two-lane room was one of their biggest rooms. But now in the Jung Hotel, you have two tremendous rooms.
Mm-hmm.
Two great big ballrooms.
This is a different kind of picture because you've got Cowbell, Maracas, and Clave's in it.

There. Yeah, that's Santo Pecoraro, way in the back on drums. This is another photograph of the Al Streaming Band, which was taken in one of the local hotels here. I don't remember which one. I think it might be the Roosevelt Hotel, and it shows Harold Geroza, who has since passed away. And just behind Harold Geroza, the sax player, is Richard Bing Crosby, who today still plays music, but he also teaches French at Holy Cross College. And behind Richard Bing Crosby, the trumpet man, is myself, Bob Coquille on string bass. And next to myself, you have Emil Fanassi, a sax player. And next to Emil, you have another sax player, Joe Grasafi, who still plays music. Emil plays a little also. Emil works in Wehrlein's up till today. He's been there for 30-some odd years repairing band instruments. Behind Emil Fanassi is Ed Dusan, who today is still a practicing attorney. Behind Eddie Dusan is Santo Pecoraro, a drummer, who incidentally is related to Big Santo Pecoraro, who is known as Santo Pecoraro, Mr. Tailgate, the trombone player. Now behind Joe Grasafi, the saxophone player, is Ted Demuth, who is a trombone player. And also, if I'm not mistaken, band director at Tulane University. Am I correct on that?
As far as I know. Right, he's been here so long, I just assume he's still there.

He was assistant band director when Morrissey was band director. Now I think Ted is band director. And next to Ted is Al Streeman at the piano. This is a photograph of the Al Streeman dance orchestra. And that was taken in 1955, and I think it's in a Roosevelt Hotel in the Grand Ballroom. Someone shot that picture. Whenever a professional photographer shoots a picture, I usually try to get a copy of it just for my recording.
So you'd come back and play a spot with him, even though you would be playing with George Girard.

Right. I would work about three nights a week with Al Streeman, and I'd work about three nights a week at the famous store with the late George Girard. Because I had to get up early in the morning and go to work, and the other bass player who was working with Girard the other three nights, he had to get about three hours sleep and then get up and play with Pinky's Dawn Busters on WWL from 5 to 7 every morning.
Now, who's playing the cowbell there?

That's the saxophone player, Harold Girosa, who since passed away a few years ago. We probably were playing a Latin tune, and Emil Finestes, Emil Finestes is playing the maracas, and Bing Richard Crosby is playing the sticks.
The clavis, yeah. The clavis. My Spanish is not too good. But, yeah, and you just barely can see Ted.

Yeah, I think Ted is today vice president of our local musicians, local here in New Orleans, Ted DeMuth. He's always an official. Also, yeah, right, he's been for years, and he's also band director here at Tulane University.
Well, and he plays with lots of bands. I've heard him play with us.
Oh, yeah. He's free.
I've heard him play with big bands.
Right, he freelances. He freelances with quite a few bands.
And sometimes he would substitute for Jack Asuna with, oh, what's his name? Frank Federico.
Frank Federico, right.
Oh, I couldn't think of Frank's name. All-round. Plays with circuses, too. When we're at his all-round guy. So now we have a celebrity with him here in this picture.

Well, back in the 30s and 40s and early 50s, you had quite a few celebrities that always came into the famous store every night. And this was shot, I don't know who shot this particular photograph. But anyway, it's a photograph taken of Lou Saino, trombone player, who later went with the Louie Primer group, traveled all around the country with Louie Primer for about 12 years before forming his own group and returning. Well, he did a little road work with his own group, Lou Saino, and then he is currently working in New Orleans at the Maison Bourbon every night with his own group. He's one of the three bands at Maison Bourbon, on Bourbon and St. Peter. He has the night shift from about 9 to 1, something like that. Next to Lou Saino is the late George Girard. I should say the late fabulous George Girard, because he had so much personality. He was a very excellent player and had so much front line personality. He completely had the audience in the palm of his hand every night. That was a great loss when George passed away at the age of 27. And next to George Girard is the late William Bendix, the movie idol who gave us so much happiness in his TV shows. And next to William Bendix is the late Harold Cooper, who recently passed away, I think within the past year. And everyone knows Harold Cooper. He played for many years and traveled all over extensively with the late Dukes of Dixieland, the original Dukes of Dixieland. And next to Harold Cooper is Marcel Bob Coquille, who was playing string bass here with the late George Girard at the famous door.
I see a photograph here of Johnny Wig's band that you took yourself. You like to take photographs?

Well, every... Once in a while? I don't get out to the Jazz Festival every year, but I try to get out when I can get out there. And when I do, I usually bring my camera. And as you know, at the Jazz Festival, which is held every year out at the fairgrounds here in New Orleans, there's about eight or ten different stages. And there's bands that are swapping around about every hour on all the various stages. And you get quite a variety of music, you've got Dixieland jazz and country and western and what have you. And now you... When I'm able to get out there, I usually go around and see all my friends and I'll shoot a few pictures of the different groups and try to make it get a little variety, you know? And this one came out real good and it's a good shot of the late Johnny Wig's and his group. And it shows Raymond Burke on clarinet, Jeff Reddick on piano, and Les Muscat, who is from England, who is a very fine banjo and a very fine guitar player, whom I had the pleasure of working with for about three years. And we have Chink Martin, the old Chink Martin that is. I say old because we have a Chink Martin Jr., who are both bass players. Chink Martin Jr. and Chink Martin Sr. And this is Chink Martin Sr., who goes back to the days of Storyville, and is a legendary jazz musician as everyone knows. And then we have Clive Wilson, who is a trumpet player from England. And you have Butsy Massico, a drummer, a fine drummer. And we have the late Jack Delaney on trombone. And this picture is shot in color, and it came out real good. And I thought I'd pass this picture on to you because it's a group of all popular jazz, New Orleans jazz musicians.
Did you ever play the festival? No, I never did.
Never once. Never did.
Well, of course, it's impossible to know how many good musicians there are in the festival. And I guess they can't include them all. Maybe they'll eventually.

I never did actually make an effort to play out there, you know, because I was always working at night. And I figured, well, I'll go out and enjoy the festival and shoot some pictures and all that. So I really never did make an effort to try to get to. I was always happy to go out there and see and listen to the music, you know.
Well, I feel the same way. I put on a hat and a rug lash so I can listen to the music instead of having to talk to people.

It's like on your day off or night off, go down and listen to some old jazz. You're not doing your family justice when you do that. So I try to enjoy a night or a week off or a day or a week off at least.

Well, the same with me. As I say, I put on a hat and dark glasses and go out there so I don't have to talk to people. Just listen to the music, hide behind the bandstands. Right. Of course, I often like to hide behind bandstands because of the amplification or the distortion up so loud. You know, incidentally, I think they've improved the sound system. They really have worked on that out there. Oh, yeah. In recent years, they seem to be finding really good people, which is nice because it doesn't happen everywhere you play.
Right. That's very true.

You can meet some real problems. Well, anyhow, there's a lot of bands that we talked about and we'd mentioned the leader. But for example, we never did talk about really who was in Sharky's band and too much of what you did with him.

Well, at the time, I was with the Sharky group. Sharky had called me like five months in advance and he said, Bob, would you like to make a road tour with me? I said, well, sure. But I said, when are you planning on leaving? And he said, oh, I'm about six months from now. I said, well, Sharky, why don't you call me about two months in advance? And then I could more officially give you an answer. You know, I mean, I don't like to plan anything six months in advance. That's pretty far away. So he says, okay. So he called me about two months in advance of the road tour. And then we started out in the dream room where he was a house band. So we worked in a dream room right on Bourbon Street, which was a popular spot at that time alternating with Sharky's Kings of Dixieland. Sharky's Kings of Dixieland was a house group where we were every night, six nights a week. And we alternated with out of town groups that came in like Jack T. Gordon and his six piece Dixieland group, you know, and groups of that caliber. And so we were in a dream room three or four months before we left for the tour. And then we went out on tour and did the round table in New York alternating with Tyree Glenn and his fine quartet. And from there we moved on to the other spots that Sharky had booked around the country, St. Louis, Toledo, Ohio and various other spots. And I really enjoyed my year with Sharky because he played a lot of Dixieland tunes that of the other bands that I'd worked with hadn't played all these Dixieland tunes. And it was, you know, you always want to learn something new and try to play all the Dixieland tunes that you can. And Sharky played nearly all the Dixieland tunes that you ever heard of. And that was, I really appreciated that. And I enjoyed working with Sharky because of his playing. And we had a good group. And Monk Hazel left with us on tour. And we had Monk Hazel, we had Joe Rodas, I should say the late Joe Rodas on trombone, myself on string bass. And I gotta think, who was the rest of the fellas?
Did you say who the clarinet player was? Oh, uh... Start at the top. The high note.

It must have been Harry Shields, I guess. Yeah, Harry Shields on clarinet. The late Harry Shields. And uh, Les Sharky on trumpet. Now let's see who am I leaving out. Joe Rodas trombone. Monk Hazel drums. Piano? We only had six men. I'm trying to think. Oh, Harvey Rubin. Harvey Rubin. Oh, yeah? Yeah, Harvey Rubin was on piano. Because he traveled in his little Volkswagen. He always had a Volkswagen in those days.
I remember.

And I traveled with Sharky and, I guess it was Sharky's car. I don't remember what kind it was. But we enjoyed it. We really had a nice tour. And the band is always Sharky's well known in New York and everywhere else.
He should be. He was at Nick's in the thirties. Oh, yeah. Mm-hmm. And uh, well, they went there before once, I think, with the Wolverine.

Right. Like I told you the other day, when we played Nick's in the Village, when I was with the Royal Alberta Bourbon Street Six, we did a lot of work at Nick's. And the first time we went there, looked in the window and they had pictures of Sharky. And in the window with his group, which was, I think, Monk Hadlen and Bill Bourgeois. And that was taken many, many years before, you know? And that picture was still in the window. So we did Nick's, oh, several times within about three or four year period. When we weren't working Nick's in Greenwich Village, we were working at the Metropole alternating with, with Cozy Cole's group. Or we'd be alternating with the late Henry Redd Allen. Or we'd be alternating with Sal Yeager's fine group. Sal Yeager is a very fine clarinet player in New York. In fact, Sal Yeager taught Steve Allen enough about clarinet to make the Benny Goodman story. And he's a very fine musician. And he really had, Benny Goodman is Sal Yeager's idol. He really loved that man. And he's a very fine clarinet player. And had his, still has his own group around New York, in New York. And he's kept busy all the time. Very fine clarinet player. So Roy Loberto and the Bourbon Street Six. And we had the pleasure working at Metropole for many years, in and out, six weeks at a pop sometimes. And then we worked with the Loberto band. We worked Las Vegas two or three times, three or four times, I should say. The Stardust Lounge and the Starlight Lounge at a Riviera in Las Vegas. All over Miami Beach. And Pittsburgh, all over Ohio, Chicago. We did flow shows in Chicago at the Edgewater Beach Hotel. Where we had the pleasure of Arthur Godfrey sitting in with us for two nights.
Oh, wow.

Because Arthur Godfrey had, happened to be in Chicago for a week with his horse, Goldie. He has a horse that does tricks. This horse, his name is Goldie. And he happened to be in Chicago that week, staying at the Edgewater Beach Hotel. Because during the day, he was performing at a stock show. His horse was performing at a stock show. And he got, and Arthur Godfrey doesn't go anywhere without his banjo. And he has a beautiful, expensive banjo. And he flipped over the banjo. We were doing two shows a night in Chicago with the Edgewater Beach Hotel in the big, I forget the name of the room. But anyway, this room holds about 800 people. And he just flipped over the ban. And he wanted to know if he could sit in with us the next night. So he sat in with us, I think, two nights in a row in a floor show. Which we really enjoyed. And he invited us to go on his daily CBS radio show in New York, which in those days came on at 10 to 11 in the morning. But we never did get up there because we didn't, we didn't, we were, in those days, we were booked like seven months in advance, you know. But he was real nice. And he just flipped over old Harry Shields, the late Harry Shields. He loved Harry Shields. Loved his plan. He says, I like that old man. And he really bragged about old Harry Shields. Who was a very good player. And of course, as everyone knows, Harry Shields was the brother of the late Larry Shields. And Larry Shields passed away many years ago in California and was responsible for writing clarinet and marmalade, plus a whole flock of other tunes. I couldn't begin a name.
You know, Arthur Godfrey had some pretty good musicians with him at the time.

Oh, pretty good. He had some great musicians with him. I went to Disney World in Orlando, Florida. Well, I went to Disneyland when I was working in Las Vegas. On our day off, Roy LaBord and I went over to Disneyland in Anaheim, California. We spent nine hours in Disneyland and really enjoyed it. And I said to myself, well, I've got to get the wife and kids to Disney World so they can see this, because this is fantastic. And when I went to Disney World, oh, many years later, because Disney World was built up many years later. And of course, it's beautiful and I think it's larger even geographically in size than Anaheim, California. But anyway, after I got back home from Disney World, I found out that these musicians that I really wanted to see were up on top of the contemporary hotel roof. Like Don Lamont, famous drummer. Oh.
Excuse me.
And Arthur Godfrey's old bass player was up there that used to do that radio show. And I can't recall his name. Traxler?
Traxler? Right. That's it.
Gene Traxler.
Gene Traxler.

That Gene Traxler was playing up on a contemporary hotel roof with the big Don Lamont band. And I was back home before I found out about that. And he was a marvelous bass player. And I think Roy LaBord and I met Don Lamont one day in Joe Glazer's office when we were up there on business to see Joe Glazer in New York. And I remember that the LaBord and the band used to be booked by ABC, which is an associated book and corporation, which at the time the late Joe Glazer was in charge.
The real is about to run out, but I remember just to mention Johnny Mintz and Lou McGarrity being in the band with a...
Right. Right. Oh, they had a very fine group.
You know, musicians and jazz.
Godfrey loves Dixieland music. He just loves it. Mm-hm.
That sort of stuff. Let's just give it a test. What's your name again?
Okay, yeah, this is Bob Coquille, back being interviewed by Dick Allen at the Tulane Jazz Archives, right here in New Orleans.
And today is November the...
And today is November 19th on a Monday morning at 9.30 in the morning.
Oh, I see. All right, well, let's try and see if we did it right this time.
Okay.
Okay, I got it on. It's going now.
All righty.
I wanted to ask you, you talked about new tunes, and that reminded me of something. What about the young musicians coming up? Do you hear any ones that play what you'd call Dixieland correctly?
Well, I haven't heard too many young groups. Actually, I haven't. I don't have the opportunity to hear them if I knew where I might be able to hear them, Dick. I'd be glad.

Well, I was just wandering around Jackson Square yesterday, and I heard Danny Rubio, who I'd never heard play tuba before, that I remember. It's a phone, actually. And he seemed to be playing a new style.
Was that right? Was that group a young group?
It was with Scotty Hill's band. Oh, Scotty Hill.
Yeah.
With Les Moskut and various people that you know.
I saw Scott Hill just a few weeks ago for the first time in many, many months. I didn't know if he had left town. Oh, no.
Mm-hm.
We got off the study, we started talking about New York.

Yeah, the meter doesn't have to go any higher than that? No, it's picking you up fine, you can see. And me. I thought it had to go up to the red line, you know, up to the red line, but I don't guess it does.
It's as loud as it'll go, to tell you the truth.
Mm-hmm, you got it on maximum.
Yeah. So it seems to be working well enough, though, to here.
Mm-hmm. Anyway. Well, that's good.
It's as good as we can do. I think we need new microphones. She's left, all these things. But these are sturdy things. They've stood up almost 20 years.
I think they're doing all right.
Yeah, anything that old can hold up. I was going to ask you about carnival balls. That's one thing we never talk much about. You mentioned playing on the truck.

Right, I did my share of carnival balls during the Alstream in 19 years. We had our share of the carnival balls. You know, I played my share of them. I did, you know, the tableau and the supper dance and the whole works. Mm-hmm. For many years, yeah. Al had his portion of it, you know. There was bands like Russ Papalia, Rene Louap, and in the old days, let's see. Johnny Detroit. Bands of that caliber and bands like that, they used to all get a certain percentage of the balls. So I feel like I did my share of them.
Never having seen one in my whole life.
You haven't seen a carnival ball?
I've never had one in to go, particularly.
Well, if you've seen one, actually, you've seen them all. Let's put it that way. Like you see one parade, you've probably seen all the parades and Mardi Gras for it. That goes.
Well, it's always impressed me that sitting there in a tuxedo and watching other people's dance is not 100%.

Well, the ladies enjoy it, I think, more than the men. It's a very colorful affair. You see, in New Orleans, you have about 65 carnival organizations here, which all the big prominent businessmen belong to. And of these 65 carnival organizations, there might be about 20 big rich carnival organizations out there at 65, and they'll each give a parade. And after the parade, then a parade goes down to the municipal auditorium, and they have the carnival ball, and they have the tableau, which always depicts some theme of the past. And then there's 12 dances or 12 call-outs, and the girls that are called out or the young ladies that are called out. It's a very formal affair. Everything is formal. The girls in the evening gowns, the ladies in the evening gowns, the men in their tails and tuxedos. And the 12 call-outs, the young ladies don't know who it is that's calling them out. And while they dance in the gentleman that belongs to the organization who is still masked, he gives the young lady a souvenir or what we call a favor. It might be a little vanity or something like that, you know. And then after the 12 call-outs, there's usually public dancing amongst everybody for about a half hour. And the ball might end at 12 o'clock or it might end at 1 o'clock in the morning. And then from 1 to 3 or from 12 to 3, there might be a supper dance at one of the hotels. By the same organization, they go to the supper dance and usually have to cost $15 or $20 to attend the supper dance because they put on a big feed. And there's a band there playing for the supper dance. So it's an all-day and all-night affair. Not all-night, not all-day, but I mean it's an all-night and all-morning affair for those who attend the supper dance. It's a very colorful affair and the women really enjoy it.
Well, how has the routine worked out? What's the first thing that goes on when you get there?

Well, the first thing that goes on is you go down to the municipal auditorium where they're usually hell. And you present. You have to have an invitation. Somebody from the carnival organization will mail you an invitation if they know you or, you know, through some friend. They might have you mail the carnival, I mean an invitation to the carnival ball. And I think they'll have RSVP on it in case you cannot make it that that invitation can be given to someone else who wants to go to a carnival ball. Because a lot of tourists coming to New Orleans have never seen a carnival ball and they're anxious to see one. So then you just go down to the municipal auditorium. You present your invitation and you go sit up in the balcony, you know, or on the ground floor if there are seats available on the ground floor. And usually the seats on the ground floor are nearest the dance floor or nearest where the tableau is going to be or for the people that are in the organization. Because then they're immediate families and that takes up quite a bit. And like I say, it's the first thing they'll do is they'll have maybe a half-hour tableau or they'll have a one-hour tableau. And it'll depict some theme of the past, you know. And they'll parade all around the room and then they'll have the king and queen of that particular carnival organization. And they're ladies or whatever they call them, ladies-in-waiting. They march all around the dance floor to the coronation waltz or one of those, you know, particular appropriate tunes. And it's a very colorful appear. And after all that goes on, then they'll have the 12 call-outs. The maskers, the people who belong to the organization are still masked. And they'll call out names, 12 names. You know, each one will call out a different lady. It might be a member of their family. It might be a very good friend. And they don't know who they're dancing with until after it's all over. When they go to the supper dance, they'll probably know. Or maybe while they're dancing, they'll tell them who they are, you know. And while they're dancing, at the end of the dance, each of them, they'll give that lady a special, what they call a favor, like a little vanity or something like that. And at the end of the 12 call-outs, then they'll allow public dance and the band will play a half hour and everybody can get out and dance, who wants to dance. And that's the end of it, you know. And the last people to march around the floor, the king and the queen, you know, and all the maids. I should say maids. I said ladies in the waiting. All the maids, oh, there's a whole gang of maids. They march around with their escort, who's not in a tuxedo, but they're in tails. They wear tails, you know, full dress, complete full dress. And it's a very colorful affair and the women really go for all that because they see all these gorgeous evening gowns and all the debutantes and all this.
Do you have to play a special march for them?

Yeah, usually it's a coronation waltz or coronation and other different, I can't think of the names of all the tunes. I can't think of the names of all the particular tunes. But you play certain numbers according to whatever theme they depict for their tableau. You have to play appropriate music for that tableau, whatever it might be, you see. I don't know. But for the marching around, you know, like the king and queen are marching around and all the maids are watching. Usually the maids are walking around with their escort. Then the last thing to march around, the last person to march around will be the king and queen, you see. Then they'll have the 12 call-outs and then they'll have the public dancing.
So it could be waltzes, foxtrots?
Oh, yeah.
What about...
Now, for the 12 call-outs, well, they might play waltzes and they might play a foxtrot. It depends on whatever they feel like playing.
Do the people have a jitterbug at a carnival ball?
Well, maybe during the public dancing for the last half hour, you know.
So they might play some peppy numbers.

Oh, yeah, sure. They might even play some peppy numbers for one of the call-outs. They won't keep playing the same tempo for the whole 12 call-outs. They'll give that variety, too. And like I say, the whole thing is a very colorful affair. Very colorful. But if you've seen one, you've more or less seen all of them.
Did you ever play tuba?
I played them. Did I ask you that? No, I never did.
Except not someone.
Never did.
That's funny. You know, just some of the nice...
Always the preferred string bass over tuba, you know.
Well, sometimes people...

I don't dislike tuba. I've heard some very fine tuba players. There's a place down in Orlando, Florida I was recommending. I knew some musicians down there in Disney World in Orlando. And the drummer said, Bob, come on down tonight in downtown Orlando. And Rosie O'Grady's. And as I mentioned before, they had a real fine group. And they had a tuba player down there. Played real fine. Well, the whole group sounded great. They had about an eight-piece band. And they had an elderly lady singing blues in the old late-timer, you know. And she was way up in her 60s, but she sang real great. Blues singer. And the place was packed. Real fine group.
By the way, where did you record with Al Hurt? What time?

With Al Hurt, we recorded right on the job at Dance Pier 600. And we recorded two... Let's see. The first Audio Fidelity we recorded was Volume 1 on Audio Fidelity. Sunday was our hardest day. On a Sunday, we used to work 4 to 8, and then 9 to 3. Now, on Sunday, we played the 4 to 8 deal in the afternoon. And then we played 9 to 3. We took an hour off, and we cut the Audio Fidelity from 4 to 10 in the morning, right on the job. In the place. We took an hour's rest and started recording. Audio Fidelity brought all the equipment down from New York, all the big setups that they shipped down here. And we recorded Volume 1 right on the job at the old Pier 600. And we finished that at 10 in the morning. And we'd be doing just fine. Sometimes plenty of them we'd do right on the first take. And then maybe we'd do the third tune. And it would be just beautiful, just fine. And then a bus would come up Bourbon Street blowing the horn. We'd have to do another take. Even though the door was closed at that time of morning, you know, at 5 in the morning, and the bus blows the horn. In those days, the buses would go up Bourbon Street, see. And a bus would come up Bourbon Street and blow the horn. We'd have to do the whole thing over. I said, somebody ought to go look out the door, see if a bus is coming.
Yeah.

So anyway, we got that squared away. We didn't have to do too many retakes. But things like that, you'd have to do a retake. We didn't want the bus horn in there. And then about two nights later, we did volume two. And then I think, I can't remember how much later we did the verve. Maybe another month later we did the verve. But it was the same situation from 4 to 10 in the morning. We'd play 9 to 3, and then from 4 to 10 in the morning, we'd cut the verve LP with Pete Fontaine on clarinet and Bob Havens on trombone. Paul Edwards, myself, Roy Zimmerman.
I'll have to get a book out and show you the write-ups because they didn't know where the records were made. They had the year listed, but that was awesome.
Well, that's...
Didn't even say what month it was.

That's the records. That's the only ones that I'm on with Al and Pete. The volume one and two of Audio Fidelity, long playing record. And a verve, long playing with Pete and Alhurt. And that verve, I understand the cover's been changed. They had all... They all had... On a verve, original verve, they had all the bus pictures of all of them and the band on the back of the cover. And on a verve, all the fellas in the group had a beard because that's when they first raised the beards. Except Paul Edwards and myself, the drummer and myself, we didn't raise beards because we have gray hair and we would have looked like Blackstone, a magician if we would have raised a beard, I guess. So instead, I think I raised a mustache for a while, but I shaved the mustache off about four months later. But that's when Al and Pete and the rest of the guys first decided on a beard. It was Al's idea about the beard because it was about three months before Mardi Gras. Al said, let's all raise a beard. And on Mardi Gras Day, we're going to play in the daytime besides at night and we'll dress like Arabs, you know. And that's when they first started and to this day, they still have it. That is, Al and Pete still have it. Pete has the Van Dyke type and, of course, Al let his grow all over. And Bob Havens and Roy Zimmerman, of course, have since shaved theirs off. And Paul Edwards and myself, well, we never did raise a beard. But to this day, Al and Pete still have their beard. And that's back in the...
Well, did they ever do anything for kicks like that?
Oh, he just thought it would be a kick to do that. That's all. It was just a deal for Mardi Gras, which was coming up three months later. And then they decided to keep the beard.
So they would enjoy Mardi Gras even if they're playing music.
Right. Right. They just decided to keep the beard after that and they never would shave it off.
It wasn't just another job for them, is what I'm getting to say.
No.
You know, some people never have any fun. Never had the impression that Pete found...

We had a lot of fun on the band. Al has a good... Al Heard has a real good sense of humor. And it was a fun night every night. And I mean, we really worked, but we enjoyed it. We worked six hours a night. We worked from nine to three. We weren't doing one show a night, four nights a week like Al was doing now. We were working six hours a night. But I enjoyed it. I really enjoyed it. Because Al made the job a fun job and we all had a good time. And Al has a heart of gold. He's a good-natured guy.
Before I forget it, I don't want to get too far from the subject. Did you ever play any Mardi Gras balls outside of New Orleans?

Yeah. When I was with the streaming group, we used to go to Mobile. Mobile has carnival balls over there. I see. And there was a hotel over there. I don't know if it's still there, but there used to be a hotel. They called the Battle House in Mobile. And we played, oh, for a few years, we played carnival balls in the Battle House in Mobile, Alabama. And, of course, I played other carnival balls on a smaller scale at different places in Jefferson Parish, you know, in different convention halls. Certain organizations up in Jefferson Parish would give a big carnival ball. But all the big carnival balls were at the municipal auditorium. Like all those are the main ones, you know. But Mobile would put on a big one in there. The last one I played in Mobile was Hell in the Armory. It was a tremendous place, you know. It was a great, big, tremendous place. But most of the balls in Mobile were at the Battle House in the old days.
Well, what was it like? Was it like a New Orleans Mardi Gras?
Just like a New Orleans Mardi Gras. Same thing.
Did it have a tambour?
Yeah. Yeah.
Call outs?
Yeah.
What about the parade?
Well, now, I don't know about the parade because I would only go over there for the carnival balls. There I'm at.
I see that.

In other words, I never saw any parades in Mobile. Now, I don't mean to say that they didn't have any. Now, maybe they had parades, too. There were a few surrounding places in the vicinity of New Orleans that had parades, I think, around Mardi Gras. But nearly everybody came to New Orleans for the Mardi Gras instead of, you know, because they knew that they was put on in New Orleans on a big scale. Now, maybe Mobile had parades. I really don't know because in those days, like I say, I was on a day job. And when I played a carnival ball in Mobile, I used to get back home at 6 o'clock in the morning, 5 o'clock in the morning, and I'd get up and go to work at 8.30. So whether they ever had carnival parades, I'm not sure.
What about in Lafayette or New Iberia? Did you ever go out there to play carnival?
I've been in New Iberia, and I've been in Lafayette. But I never would play any carnival balls in New Iberia or Lafayette.
Any of the towns out to the southwest?
The only other place, like I say, we're in maybe in Kenner, Harahan, you know, which are in Jefferson Parish. Used to give a few carnival balls.
Did you ever go to Washington, D.C.?
Oh, yeah. I played the annual Mardi Gras ball there with Al Hurd in the Mayflower Hotel.
Yeah, Al, every year they usually select a New Orleans band.

And I don't know what's going on in the last few years, but in the days of Al Hurd, when I was with Al Hurd, rather, around that era of time that we were getting a band from New Orleans, I think Senator Long was always in charge, I think, of, I had a lot to do with anyway, the annual Mardi Gras ball, which is usually held in the Mayflower every year. And, well, during that two years I was with Al Hurd, we went up there, they flew us up there to do the Mardi Gras ball, put us up in the Mayflower overnight, and it was a big, spectacular thing. Everybody was there from the vice president on down. I don't think the president was there, but I think from the vice president on down, I think it was there. I can't even remember who was the vice president at the time. Whoever was the vice president in 56 or 57 or 58, I guess. But all the dignitaries would have, the senators, the congressmen, what have you. It's a big deal in Washington, this annual affair.
Is that the same as here? I mean, do they have a tableau or call outs?

I don't know if they had a tableau or not, because I know we rode into the main room on a float. They had a small float, you know, where the band was on top of float, the whole band. And we rode into the room with music playing. Now whether they had a tableau or not, I don't know. But I know they have a, oh, they sent up a whole gang of girls from New Orleans. And it's a very colorful affair also up there. But I don't recall if they have a tableau or not. They might have a tableau.
I wanted to go on to that. I had an invitation.

Well, your best deal is to make one in New Orleans. Try to get to one in New Orleans. And if you see one in New Orleans, like the Twelfth Night Revelers or any big one at the municipal auditorium, you ought to try to get there once. It's a formal affair. Put on a tuxedo one night and just go sit down and observe the whole deal.
Sometimes they're other than that.

And then you can say, well, all the rest are pretty much the same. If not identical, pretty close anyway. But you'll get a kick out of it. If you've never seen it, I would recommend that everybody see at least one carnival ball. It's a very colorful affair.
Well, my ex-wife just didn't want to go. And it was, you know, the invitation.
I don't know. I think the women enjoy it way more than the men do because they love to look at somebody else's evening gown. And they think it's a very colorful affair. It is a very colorful affair.
Back to your records, too. Another thing. Who was Phil Dooley? I never did know him. He sang with Norman?

Well, Joe Merez knew Phil Dooley. I hadn't known him until a record session. I don't know if he's from New Orleans, but he came down and he did one of these Southland records with us. And he sang, if I remember right, on the recording. And Joe Merez knew him real well. I didn't know Phil Dooley until I cut the record.
But did you know if he was an emcee or? He just sang. That's all you knew about him, huh?
I don't even know. I don't even remember if Phil played a musical instrument. I think he just sang. I think he just sang with the band.
There's so many people like that around him.
Yeah.
So many of the emcees did sing.
Mm-hmm.
And stuff.
I don't even know if Phil Dooley was from New Orleans.
Yeah. Wow. Did you ever...
Did you have that Southland record?
Yeah, we've got it here.
You've got it?
And one of the books says it has a banjo on it, but I never heard the banjo.
Well, on one of the recordings I made, I think Joe... Not Joe Valenti. Joe... Oh, what's this guy's name?
What did he...
Played guitar with us. Fine guitar player. Oh, what's this man's name?
The only Joe I know who plays guitar is Joe Caprera.
That's it.
He worked a lot for Joe Merez.

I'm glad you're interviewing me, Dick, because you can remember all these names. Well, this is your business to remember all those names, I guess. Yeah. Joe Caprera. Yeah. Fine guitar player. I think he's on one of the Southlands that I'm on. Fine guitarists. Yeah.
Well, sometimes they get those things mixed up.

Joe Caprera had a great band at one time, and they used to work the old Beverly Country Club, but it was under a different name, I think, at the time. I'm not sure. And then Joe Caprera worked a long time in Hot Springs, Arkansas with a great group. Everybody said he had a really good band. Yeah, he did, and he worked Hot Springs, Arkansas for a good while. I still see Joe once in a while, not too often.
I think he's still driving for Shane.
He drives Funeral Home, Lumacine.
The last time I was there, I think, was maybe in May.
I think the last time.
And I didn't see him, but then I had other things on my mind.

That's the only time I see Joe now is when I attend a funeral. He's usually one of the emblems. I say emblems. One of the lumazine drivers. And he still remembers me real well. We always have a little chat every time I see him.
And who was in Almond Kay's band?

Almond Kay had a fine little group at the Fountain Blue Hotel here on Tulane and Calton. And we played in the La Chondelle Lounge there for about nine months, I think, close to ten months. And in that group, we had Almond Kay, the band leader, and the trumpet man, plays fine trumpet. And we had Jerry Bouquet on clarinet, antenna saxophone, and flute, very fine musician. And we had Joe Clark on drums. And we had Bob Doyle on piano. And Bob plays marvelous piano, very fine piano man. He and I used to work together many years before at a small lounge. I think that was it. Did I name all that? Let's see. Joe Clark drums, myself, string bass. Bob Doyle piano, Almond Kay trumpet. And Jerry Bouquet on tenor sax, flute, and clarinet. And we played for dancing there in the La Chondelle Lounge, beautiful room. That's where Ronnie Cole is currently working with his group.
When did you switch to this electronic type bass?

I switched over to, well, nearly everyone on Bourbon Street at the time, it was playing electric bass, or some people refer to it as guitar bass. So I figured, well, I have to keep up with the times. I'm getting to be an old man now. If I want to keep working, I better switch over. So anyway, I switched over, sat in my den for about two weeks and practiced till about four o'clock in the morning for about two weeks, and then I brought it on the job and started playing it. Went through a couple of method books. But after, I used to sit up till about four, five o'clock in the morning and doing it for a couple of weeks, and I got by good enough to bring it on the job.
Do you feel like it?

So I would say about six years, seven, maybe close to seven years. Well, I'll be very honest with you, Dick. I played string bass about 37 years, and I always did like bass. I love string bass, and I love electric bass also. What I like about guitar bass, being an old guitar player myself, guitar bass came a little easier to me than I thought it would. And I find it to be very clean in playing, and I don't have to lug that big bass fiddle around. And I always did like it, but I was, even when I played string bass, I liked guitar bass, but I was jealous of it, like all, I think string bass players are jealous of it. Say, oh, that electricity. If you have a power failure, then what? You know, I thought of that. That's the first thing I thought of. But you know, the first one I heard, I was playing at the famous store with Le George Girard, and this is back, way back. And Freddie Bell and the Bell Boys came down to the dream room, on Bourbon Street, which the dream room is no more now. It's Wilson's Restaurant now. And before Wilson's Restaurant, it was your father's mustache. And then before that, it was a good old popular dream room, which had fine, good Dixieland music in it, and T. Gordon and everybody else, and Sharky and all the good bands. Well, Freddie Bell came down. Freddie Bell and the Bell Boys came down to the dream room with about an eight-piece band. And Freddie Bell is a marvelous entertainer. He does a lot of work in Las Vegas nowadays and for the past few years. A great entertainer. And he had an electric bass player with him. And it just flipped me. It was the first time I saw electric bass or saw anybody playing electric bass. Of course, it looks like a guitar almost, and you know. But anyway, I liked it, but I would never tell anybody that I liked it because I was actually, I was jealous of it. I said, oh, that electricity, man, suppose that goes out, then you're lost in a fog. I liked it, but I wouldn't tell anybody. I was really jealous of it. And then later on, when I played Las Vegas the first time, we added a girl vocalist. We did Stardust. They liked girls on the bandstand in Vegas, so our booking agent added a girl vocalist. Sally Corby added to our group. And Sally Corby is a very fine vocalist in Las Vegas. Her husband used to play one of the twin pianos at the Sands, I think it was. He's since passed away. He had a massive heart attack. Her husband passed away. Well, Sally Corby used to sing with all the big groups that hit Vegas, like, oh, Dixie groups that went there, like the Bob Crosby Band, some of the other grand Dixie groups of that caliber. They had Sally Corby. So she worked quite a bit with all the Dixie groups. And when she wasn't doing that, she would be in a Red Skelton chorus line when he would be performing in one of the big runs, because Sally could dance and sing, you see. So anyway, Sally Corby joined the Royal Laborator group for the whole month that we were there, and even the second year, when we went back again at the Stardust. And the third year, we didn't use the vocalists at the Riviera Starlight Lounge. Well, anyway, Freddie Bell does a lot of work in Las Vegas. And Sally Corby's daddy, she says, Bob, why don't you come down in downtown Las Vegas? My daddy has a loan office down there. And she says, there's a lot of things down there that look pretty good. Why don't you go look around? So I went on down the next day, and they had an electric base in the window. You know? And I could have gotten an electric base at that time, which would have been like 10 or 12 years sooner, but I still didn't buy it. I liked it, but I was jealous of it. And to think that I could have bought that bass then, you know, for about $75, I could have bought that Fender Jazz Bass in Las Vegas, but it was about 12 years later, I guess, before I bought one.
Well, does it change your plan?

I really like it. I really like it, because I find it clean, the notes are real clean, and I just forgot about the electrical end of it having to phase out, because I've got a spare. I can always jump to a spare, you know, even though I keep the spare at home, you know what I mean? But I could have a spare on the job in a half hour's time.
Well, you never had a problem.
It's never failed me yet. Yeah. It's never failed me yet.
I wish I could say the same for tape recording.

That used to be my main worry about bass guitar. Well, if you have a power failure, or you blow a fuse, well, all bass guitar players carry spare fuses. Stick a spare fuse. A spare fuse would be in your amplifier, not in your bass. And I haven't even blown a fuse since I'm playing guitar, bass, and it's about seven years. It's never let me down yet. So I'm real happy with it now. I enjoy playing it. And it's much easier to get around. It's like carrying a violin now instead of a great big bass violin.
Well, can you get around on it physically and play more notes or less notes?
Well, like I say, being an old guitar player, it came easier to me.
Yeah, so you could...
I would say it's much easier than string bass. It is. To me, it's easier than string bass.
Yeah.
String bass is hard.
Yeah. Well, I noticed that it does change the line.

And I played string bass 37 years. And this has frets on it, and the string bass doesn't have frets. So, you know, and being an old guitar player for four years, it came to me quicker than I anticipated. So I really like it. I can truthfully say I really like guitar, bass. I know a lot of the old timers like the string bass now. And I don't dislike string bass. I still love string bass, and I love to hear good bass players. I'm not putting down string bass at all because I played it for 37 years, and I really like it. But in my particular case, I'm very happy with the guitar bass because there's quite a few of them around the country. Even the Doc Severson band playing guitar bass now. You find more and more of them every year. I really like it.
Do you ever use the fuzz tone and those effects? Anything like that?
How do you mean the fuzz tone?
Well, they have something switch. It's a pedal.
Oh, no. You're talking about electric guitars now.
No.
No.
I've seen...
Not for bass.
Joey's French. Get some very strange sounds out of them.
Oh, all he's just doing is running his hand up and down.

segments.chapter: Opening and photographs of New Orleans bands
segments.title: Reel change and chat about the crawfish tie
segments.summary: Fourth reel; the interview resumes on Monday morning at the Tulane Jazz Archives, with joking about the interviewer's crawfish tie.

segments.chapter: Opening and photographs of New Orleans bands
segments.title: Clean versus rough playing in dance and Dixieland bands
segments.summary: Coquille describes dance-band reading versus faking jazz, his 1953 switch to Dixieland on Bourbon Street, and says he likes both clean and rough bands depending on the group.

segments.chapter: Opening and photographs of New Orleans bands
segments.title: Photo of the Al Streeman band on the Jung Hotel roof
segments.summary: Coquille identifies players in a 1930s photo he took on the Jung Hotel roof garden, and they talk about the hotel's big ballrooms.

segments.chapter: Opening and photographs of New Orleans bands
segments.title: Photo of the 1955 Al Streeman orchestra at the Roosevelt Hotel
segments.summary: He names the sidemen in a 1955 Roosevelt Hotel photo and explains that he split his week between Streeman and George Girard.

segments.chapter: Opening and photographs of New Orleans bands
segments.title: Latin percussion in the photo and Ted DeMuth
segments.summary: Who is playing cowbell, maracas and claves in the photo, and a note on Ted DeMuth, Tulane band director and union officer.

segments.chapter: Opening and photographs of New Orleans bands
segments.title: Photo of celebrities at the Famous Door with George Girard
segments.summary: Coquille names Lou Salino, George Girard, William Bendix and Harold Cooper in a photo taken at the Famous Door, with praise for Girard.

segments.chapter: Opening and photographs of New Orleans bands
segments.title: Johnny Wiggs band photo from the Jazz Festival
segments.summary: A color photo Coquille took of Johnny Wiggs's group at the Jazz Festival, with the players named.

segments.chapter: Opening and photographs of New Orleans bands
segments.title: Never playing the Jazz Festival; enjoying it as a listener
segments.summary: He never tried to play the festival because he worked nights, and prefers to enjoy it as a spectator; they discuss the sound system.

segments.title: Touring with Sharkey Bonano's band
segments.summary: Sharkey's call about a road tour, the Dream Room job, the Round Table in New York, and the band's personnel.

segments.title: Nick's, the Metropole and road work with Roy Liberto's Bourbon Street Six
segments.summary: Playing Nick's in the Village, the Metropole with Cozy Cole and others, Las Vegas and the Chicago Edgewater Beach Hotel with Liberto.

segments.title: Arthur Godfrey sits in at the Edgewater Beach Hotel
segments.summary: Godfrey, in Chicago with his horse, sits in with the band for two nights and praises Harry Shields.

segments.title: Disneyland, Disney World and Gene Traxler
segments.summary: Coquille tells of visiting Disneyland with Liberto and missing Don Lamont and Gene Traxler at Disney World.

segments.title: Booking through ABC and Joe Glazer; Godfrey's love of Dixieland
segments.summary: Liberto's band was booked by ABC under Joe Glazer; the reel runs out as they mention Mintz and McGarrity and Godfrey's taste for Dixieland.

segments.title: New tape test and date
segments.summary: Testing the recorder and restating the date and place.

segments.title: Young Dixieland groups and Scotty Hill's band
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about young Dixieland players; Coquille has heard few, and they mention Danny Rubio and Scotty Hill.

segments.title: Microphone levels and tape chatter
segments.summary: Checking the recording level and the age of the equipment.

segments.title: Playing carnival balls with Al Streeman
segments.summary: Coquille played many carnival balls with Streeman; other bands got shares too; he describes the ball's colour and the carnival organizations.

segments.title: How a carnival ball runs: tableau, call-outs and music
segments.summary: Step by step: invitations, the tableau, the king and queen, the twelve call-outs, public dancing, and the music played at each stage.

segments.title: Never played tuba; a tuba band in Orlando
segments.summary: He preferred string bass to tuba, and recalls a good group with a tuba and a blues singer at Rosie O'Grady's in Orlando.

segments.title: Recording Audio Fidelity and Verve LPs live at Pier 600 with Al Hirt
segments.summary: Recording on the job at Pier 600 after the shift, with bus-horn retakes, then the Verve LP with Pete Fountain and others.

segments.title: The Hirt band's beards and the fun of the job
segments.summary: The beard idea for Mardi Gras, who kept theirs, and Coquille's praise of Hirt's humor and the six-hour nights.

segments.chapter: Carnival balls away from New Orleans
segments.title: Carnival balls in Mobile and around Louisiana
segments.summary: Playing balls at the Battle House in Mobile and in Jefferson Parish; not in Lafayette or New Iberia.

segments.chapter: Carnival balls away from New Orleans
segments.title: Mardi Gras ball in Washington with Al Hirt
segments.summary: Flown to the Mayflower Hotel to play the annual Mardi Gras ball, riding in on a float; advice to see one New Orleans ball.

segments.title: Singer Phil Dooley and the Southland record
segments.summary: Coquille knew little about Phil Dooley, who sang on a Southland record, and they discuss whether a banjo is on it.

segments.title: Guitarist Joe Caprera
segments.summary: Recalling Joe Caprera's guitar playing, his band, work in Hot Springs, and his job driving for a funeral home.

segments.title: Almond Kay's group at the Fontainebleau
segments.summary: The personnel of Almond Kay's band in the La Chandelle Lounge.

segments.title: Switching to electric bass and the jealousy of an old string bass player
segments.summary: How and why he switched, first seeing electric bass with Freddie Bell, and the Fender he passed up in Las Vegas.

segments.title: Liking electric bass: reliability, ease and effects
segments.summary: He finds the electric bass clean and easy, never failed him, and still loves string bass.
